data.title: Jánovce–Machalovce – a Púchov culture hillfort in the Spiš region
data.excerpt: South of the village of Jánovce rises an unforested hill called Hradisko, where a fortified acropolis of about 3 hectares and a bailey of up to 30 hectares place the site among the larger hillforts and oppida of central Europe. The finds of the Púchov culture include a unique bronze figurine of a naked Celt with gold eyes and more than a thousand silver coins of the Cotini.
data.metaDescription: A hillfort above Jánovce: a 3 ha acropolis and a 30 ha bailey of the Púchov culture, with a bronze figurine of a Celt with gold eyes among the finds.

children.text: South of the village of Jánovce and its hamlet of Machalovce rises an unforested hill called Hradisko, which conceals one of the most important archaeological sites in the region. This place, with its rich history and occupied as early as prehistory, was used most intensively in the Late Iron Age (the period of the La Tène culture) and in the Early Roman period. It was then that a massive fortified hillfort of the Púchov culture arose here.

The centre of the hillfort was a fortified acropolis of roughly 3 hectares, built on the summit of the hill. Its defensive system consisted of two ramparts, probably made of timber structures filled with earth and stones, with a ditch running between them. Access to the hillfort was provided by at least one gateway, situated in the northern or north-eastern part, as suggested by the surviving earthworks and by the results of geophysical survey. The gateway and the fortification may have been supplemented by watchtowers, although their precise form still remains shrouded in mystery.

Below the acropolis extended the bailey – an extensive area of up to 30 hectares in the locality known as Pod Hradiskom, naturally protected by the Sihoť stream and by steep slopes. Archaeological survey here revealed traces of sunken settlement features, which had been disturbed by the cultivation of the land. In addition, north-west of the acropolis lies another potential part of the bailey, in the locality known as Nad Jánovcami, which is of similar size. Archaeological finds from this area are, however, still lacking, mainly because it is used as pasture.

The extent and character of the Jánovce hillfort place it among the larger hillforts and oppida of central Europe. Similar centres are known from sites such as Liptovská Sielnica–Liptovská Mara, or the Celtic oppida in Bratislava, at Devín and at Zemplín.

The first archaeological finds from the Jánovce hillfort were recovered as early as the 19th century, when local inhabitants came across pottery, iron slag and other items connected with metallurgical production. Interest in the site deepened only in the second half of the 20th century, chiefly thanks to the development of agriculture in the locality known as Pod Hradiskom. Important finds began to be handed over to museums, which was also recorded by Vojtech Budinský-Krička in his report of 1958.

Since 1996 the archaeological investigation of this site has been pursued systematically by Marián Soják of the Institute of Archaeology of the Slovak Academy of Sciences. Thanks to his work, the assemblage of finds has been enlarged by numerous coins of the La Tène period and by many other valuable artefacts. At the turn of the 20th and 21st centuries further archaeologists joined the research and revealed new details about life on the hillfort.

In recent years the hillfort has, sadly, also become a target of illegal metal detecting. For this reason an effort to have it declared a national cultural monument was launched in 2020. As part of these activities, extensive investigations began under the direction of Matúš Hudák of the Archeológia Spiš company, in cooperation with the Department of Archaeology of the Faculty of Arts of Constantine the Philosopher University in Nitra, the Regional Monuments Board in Žilina and the Septentrio society, the Hradiská civic association, Archeo Moravia and other volunteers.

Between 2020 and 2022 a systematic surface survey was carried out below the hillfort, which produced more than 1,500 archaeological finds. These document continuous occupation of the place from prehistory through the early historical periods to the Middle Ages and the modern era.

In the spring of 2021 a geophysical survey in the form of magnetometry was carried out, which recorded the course of the rampart defences as well as several marked anomalies. These point to the presence of metal objects and of burnt structures. On the basis of these results, the first trial archaeological excavation of the north-western part of the hillfort was conducted in 2021 and 2022.

The excavation was led by Mária Hudáková of the Spiš Museum in cooperation with archaeologists from Archeológia Spiš, Constantine the Philosopher University in Nitra and the Museum in Kežmarok. The test trenching was interdisciplinary in character – it involved geodetic survey, archaeobotanical and archaeozoological analyses, metallographic and petrographic studies of the finds, and specialised geomagnetic measurements.

Thanks to this teamwork it has been possible to sketch a picture of life and defence on this fascinating hillfort, which has a chance of becoming an even more significant part of our cultural heritage.

children.text: Finds from the Púchov culture hillfort at Jánovce

The Púchov culture hillfort at Jánovce is an important archaeological site which offers valuable insights into the life of the Cotini, a Celtic people who settled the north of present-day Slovakia. Occupation of this place came to an end some 1,800 years ago, but the archaeological finds testify to a rich everyday life as well as to dramatic historical events.

The excavations demonstrated traces of occupation as early as the 3rd century BC, while the most intensive period of use of the hillfort falls in the Late La Tène period and the beginning of the Roman period. An important discovery is the evidence of a severe fire of the fortification: the burnt rampart with its stone wall and wooden posts can be dated to the 1st century BC. The burnt layers also contained military items and contact material which suggests clashes with the Dacians and Germanic peoples.

From the bailey comes a unique bronze figurine of a naked Celt with gold eyes, wearing the characteristic neck ring (torc), representing a realistically modelled male figure without a moustache, which contrasts with the classical written descriptions. Also exceptional is a fragment of a glass bead depicting a human face, the only one of its kind in Slovakia. Together with further finds of beads of amber, glass and sea coral it points to developed crafts and long-distance contacts.

The Cotini were skilled craftsmen – evidence of jewellery such as finger rings, earrings, bracelets and temple rings suggests their feeling for aesthetics. Decorative pins and hair rings were also found, which testifies to stylised hairdressing. The houses were predominantly of log construction, with sandstone footings and hearths lined with stones. In the living quarters, pottery vessels, tools and an iron key in the shape of the letter T were found, intended for a sliding locking system – evidence of the practical aspects of everyday life.

children.text: Even after the demise of the hillfort the area was partly used. Further finds come from the 1st century AD, but they disappear in the following period, which may be connected with a shift of the population to other hillforts. The Cotini finally ceased to exist as a separate entity at the end of the 2nd century AD, when the Romans resettled them in Pannonia after the Marcomannic Wars.
Diet and activities of the inhabitants of the Púchov culture hillfort

The archaeological finds from Jánovce provide valuable insights into the diet of the hillfort's inhabitants. Of the more than 140 fragments of animal bone recovered, remains of cattle, horses and sheep or goats were identified. These animals were the main source of meat, milk and wool. Pork appeared on the hillfort only rarely, and mainly in a ritual context. Archaeobotanical analyses also documented plant food – above all millet and peas, but also wheat, barley and broad beans. Meals were prepared in pottery pots with an admixture of graphite, which increased their resistance to heat. Vessels such as jugs, cups and so-called fumigators served not only for dining but probably also for keeping fire alive or for ritual purposes.

Agricultural activity is documented by finds of stone querns, in which grain was ground into flour, as well as by tools such as an iron mattock tip. Food was stored in large storage vessels with a characteristically shaped neck and with handles. Craft production was developed above all in the field of metalworking – crucibles, casting moulds, slag and iron tools were found. The finds also confirm the processing of iron ore from local sources.

Another branch of craft was textile production, documented by finds of spindle whorls and by the weaving of cloth on looms, whose existence is attested by clay loom weights. Also important were the finds of luxury painted pottery of the 1st century BC, which point to local pottery production, probably in the Spiš region itself. From the sphere of armament come iron arrowheads, spearheads and riding spurs, and evidence of the existence of a military contingent for the protection of the hillfort.
Trade and contacts of the Púchov culture hillfort

The Púchov culture hillfort at Jánovce was not only a centre of agricultural and craft production, but also an important point in the trade network. Trade is confirmed above all by the numerous finds of coins – more than 1,000 pieces of local silver Cotinian issues (for example the Liptovská Mara, Veľký Bysterec and Spiš types). Imported coins were also discovered, for instance Balkan denarii, which testifies to supra-regional contacts.

Luxury goods were probably imported as well – pottery, glass and various metal objects. Finds of particular bronze brooches, finger rings with glass settings and imported belt parts point to contacts with the Pannonian, Balkan and northern Polish milieu (for example representatives of the Przeworsk culture). Trade contacts were thus spread right across central Europe.

Graphite may also have served for exchange – an exceptional material used in pottery, whose local sources could have been important for the surrounding region. Another important trade commodity was probably the local production of high-quality pottery, including painted vessels.
